stories.headline: Update: Federal Judge Questions USPS Over Mail Ballot Plan as Election Day Nears
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Boston sharply questioned the U.S. Postal Service on Thursday over its plan to regulate mail ballots for the November midterm elections, saying she has received no information from the agency about how the rules would actually be implemented. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani is weighing whether to extend a 14-day temporary restraining order that blocks the USPS from moving forward with a plan tied to a Trump executive order. The order expires next week, just as states begin mailing ballots to voters — roughly 70 days before Election Day.

The Justice Department told the judge the administration would likely seek emergency relief from the Supreme Court by the end of the week to allow the plan to proceed. The Supreme Court previously overturned an earlier Talwani injunction in August, ruling it was premature because USPS had not yet published formal regulations — which the agency subsequently did, prompting Democrats and voting rights groups to re-file suits.

Opponents of the plan, including election officials, argue they cannot realistically comply with the new directives, which require states to submit ballot envelope designs for USPS approval and upload voter lists to an online portal before any mail ballots are sent. They also argue the president lacks constitutional authority to set election rules, a power reserved to states and Congress. The administration contends the rules are necessary to ensure ballot integrity.

The case is one of the most consequential election-law fights of the cycle, with some states already having sent mail ballots. A Supreme Court decision on the administration's emergency application is expected within days and could determine the rules under which tens of millions of Americans cast their midterm votes.

stories.headline: Billionaire Leon Black Sues House Oversight Committee, Defies Epstein Subpoena
stories.summary:
Billionaire private equity investor Leon Black filed a federal lawsuit Thursday seeking to block congressional subpoenas and refused to appear before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee for a scheduled deposition on his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black, co-founder of Apollo Global Management, had been subpoenaed in June after walking out of a voluntary appearance before the same panel. He argues in the lawsuit that the committee lacks the authority to compel him to hand over non-disclosure agreements related to women in Epstein's orbit.

The committee's Republican chairman, Rep. James Comer, said he would consult with committee members about next steps in light of Black's defiance. A Democrat on the panel called for holding Black in contempt of Congress for ignoring two separate subpoenas. Black has denied any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he had a years-long financial relationship.

The Epstein investigation has drawn bipartisan attention, though members differ on its scope and targets. Republicans have focused the probe on Epstein's broader network of associates, while some Democrats have questioned the committee's priorities. The defiance of a congressional subpoena by a prominent financial figure raises the stakes for the committee's ability to conduct oversight.

The legal challenge sets up a confrontation that could move quickly through the courts given the committee's ongoing investigation. Black's lawsuit asks a federal judge to rule that the subpoenas are improper — a fight that could delay or derail the deposition indefinitely.

stories.headline: Treasury Issues Rules Threatening Tax-Exempt Status of Schools With Race-Based Policies
stories.summary:
The U.S. Treasury Department on Thursday released new rules that would strip schools — including universities and private K-12 institutions — of their tax-exempt status if they consider race in admissions decisions, scholarship awards, or other programs. The move escalates the Trump administration's campaign against race-conscious policies in education following the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling against affirmative action in college admissions. Hundreds of educational institutions could face significant financial consequences if their policies are deemed non-compliant.

The rules represent one of the most far-reaching federal actions to reshape higher education finance since the affirmative action rulings. Supporters argue the regulations enforce equal treatment under the law and extend the logic of the Supreme Court's decision to financial incentives, ensuring institutions do not circumvent the ruling through race-based scholarships or other programs. Critics contend the rules go well beyond what the court required and amount to federal overreach into institutional governance.

For universities, losing tax-exempt status would dramatically increase their tax burden and could jeopardize the tax deductibility of charitable donations — a major source of endowment funding. Legal challenges are widely expected, and advocacy groups for higher education have already signaled they will contest the regulations in court.

The announcement comes amid broader administration efforts to reshape college campuses, including executive orders on diversity programs and the withholding of federal research grants. The rules put institutions in the position of choosing between race-conscious financial aid programs and their tax status — a choice that could accelerate changes to how schools structure scholarships and admissions support.

stories.headline: More Than 80 Migrants Feared Dead After Boat Adrift 27 Days Off Canary Islands
stories.summary:
Spanish maritime rescue teams on Wednesday recovered a stricken vessel roughly 65 nautical miles southwest of Gran Canaria that had been adrift in the Atlantic Ocean for approximately 27 days. Rescuers found 44 survivors and five bodies aboard the boat, which is believed to have departed The Gambia in West Africa in early August carrying 127 people. Human rights activist Helena Maleno Garzón, founder of the charity Caminando Fronteras, said 83 people are feared to have perished.

Three of the survivors were airlifted to hospital in critical condition, while the remainder were transported by sea to Gran Canaria, arriving in the early hours of Thursday. Rescuers were unable to recover the five bodies found on board due to rough sea conditions, including 20-knot winds and 2.5-meter waves. All 44 survivors are men from sub-Saharan Africa.

The Atlantic route from West Africa to Spain's Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year, facing treacherous seas, strong currents, and extreme distances from the African coast. Fernando Clavijo, head of the Canary Islands regional government, called the continued loss of life "intolerable" and said the Atlantic should not be accepted as "a death trap."

The incident underscores the ongoing human toll of irregular migration across the central Atlantic, a route that has seen surging crossings in recent years as migrants seek alternatives to more heavily patrolled Mediterranean routes. The tragedy is likely to renew calls for greater search-and-rescue capacity and international cooperation on migration management.

stories.headline: Vance to Deliver First White House Press Briefing in Six Weeks as Press Secretary Role Remains Vacant
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance is scheduled to hold the White House's first press briefing in 42 days on Thursday afternoon, stepping in for a press secretary role left vacant since Karoline Leavitt's departure at the end of August. The briefing, set for 1 p.m. EDT, marks an unusual elevation of the vice president to a public communications function typically handled by a press secretary.

Vance is also expected to speak on a new domestic manufacturing training initiative called the Foundry School, a project under the State Department's Pax Silica program aimed at developing entrepreneurs, engineers, and industrial leaders as part of the administration's focus on domestic production.

The briefing comes as the administration faces mounting pressures on multiple fronts: the ongoing U.S.-Iran war, rising Treasury yields, the approach of November midterm elections, and a court block on the administration's executive order restricting birthright citizenship. A federal judge in Maryland on Wednesday issued a preliminary injunction halting the order, citing the Supreme Court's earlier ruling against a similar measure.

The extended gap between press briefings has drawn attention from media observers amid a period of significant foreign policy and domestic turbulence. The White House has not announced a timeline for naming a permanent press secretary to replace Leavitt.

stories.headline: Update: NBA Hands LA Clippers Record $30 Million Fine, Five Draft Picks, and Owner Suspension in Kawhi Leonard Pay Scandal
stories.summary:
The NBA has issued the largest financial penalty in league history against the Los Angeles Clippers, fining the franchise $30 million and stripping it of five first-round draft picks between 2029 and 2033 for violating salary cap rules in connection with star player Kawhi Leonard. Owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended from all league and team activities for 12 months, and team president Gillian Zucker received a one-year suspension without pay for providing misleading statements to investigators.

The league's investigation, opened in September 2025 following a report by podcast journalist Pablo Torre, found that Leonard pressured the Clippers into securing off-court income opportunities that circumvented salary cap rules through a $28 million endorsement contract with Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC. Leonard himself was fined $700,000 and issued a statement saying he accepts full responsibility while maintaining he acted in good faith and had no knowledge of intent to circumvent league rules.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver called the violations "flagrant" and said the severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the misconduct. The Clippers, described by the league as a prior offender of salary-cap circumvention rules, will also be subject to a five-year compliance and monitoring program.

The Clippers vehemently rejected the findings, calling the investigation "heavily biased" and saying the league's private communications differed from its public announcement. The team said it would appeal through every available avenue. Leonard, 35, is now expected to complete a previously stalled move to the Toronto Raptors following the conclusion of the investigation.

stories.headline: Putin Says Ukraine Conflict Cannot Be Resolved by Outside Nations, Cites Threats as Complicating Peace Talks
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok that Russia and Ukraine maintain contacts but gave little indication that meaningful progress toward a peace deal is underway. Putin said the conflict must be resolved by the nations directly involved, pushing back against the role of Western powers in shaping any settlement.

Putin specifically cited Ukraine's threats to disrupt air traffic to Russia as complicating the bilateral prospects for negotiations. The remarks came amid reports that Ukraine has been targeting infrastructure connected to Russia's military operations, including sites linked to satellite and space-based systems that support the war effort.

The statements add to a pattern of public Russian signaling that is simultaneously open to dialogue while resistant to the framework Western governments and Ukraine have proposed for any ceasefire or settlement. Earlier this week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent met with Russia's finance minister at the G20, signaling some American openness to engagement with Moscow, though no diplomatic breakthrough has been announced.

The war in Ukraine continues alongside the separate and ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict, stretching Western alliance resources and attention. European leaders have separately vowed a coordinated response to Russian provocations, including a drone attack blamed on Moscow near Leipzig airport in Germany.

stories.headline: Sharpeville Massacre Survivors Launch Legal Fight to Overturn Apartheid-Era Immunity Law 66 Years After Killings
stories.summary:
Survivors of the 1960 Sharpeville massacre announced Thursday a legal case seeking to overturn a South African indemnity law passed in 1961 that shielded police officers who killed at least 69 peaceful protesters from prosecution. The lawsuit represents the first formal legal effort to strip away that protection and pursue accountability for the killings, which became a pivotal moment in the global anti-apartheid movement.

Among the plaintiffs is 86-year-old Abraham Mofokeng, who still has a bullet lodged in his spine from the day police opened fire on thousands of demonstrators protesting South Africa's pass laws, which required Black citizens to carry identity documents restricting their movement. "We weren't seen as people," Mofokeng told the BBC, describing the conditions that drove demonstrators to the police station that day.

South Africa's post-apartheid government established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to address crimes committed under white-minority rule, but survivors say the process delivered no criminal accountability for Sharpeville. The indemnity law has remained on the books, and none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted despite the massacre's international infamy.

The case raises significant questions about the limits of transitional justice mechanisms and whether decades-old immunity laws can be challenged in court. Human rights advocates are watching the case as a potential precedent for similar efforts across other post-conflict societies where perpetrators were shielded by laws passed in the waning days of repressive regimes.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Strikes U.S. Allies in Gulf After American Forces Hit Wedding Party, Kill Four
stories.summary:
Iran launched missile and drone attacks against American bases and allies across the Gulf region on Wednesday, following a new wave of U.S. strikes along Iran's southern coast that killed at least 18 people, according to Iran's health minister. The escalation included a U.S. strike that hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, a small town overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, killing two women and two children aged 4 and 16, and wounding at least 68 others. Iran said it then struck targets in Kuwait and the UAE in retaliation.

The U.S. military also struck two Iranian government tankers as part of Tuesday's operations — the first time American forces have hit Iranian tankers in retaliation for attacks on shipping, rather than to enforce the naval blockade. U.S. officials confirmed this was part of a new "tanker for tanker" policy approved by President Trump to deter Iranian attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

President Trump said at the White House that the renewed campaign would not last long but threatened to hit Tehran "very hard" if the Strait of Hormuz conflict remains unresolved. Trump also downplayed the war's potential impact on Republican candidates in the November midterms, saying he plans to campaign for GOP candidates in competitive races in Alaska and Texas.

Trump faces mounting pressure to avoid an escalatory spiral, with the U.S. military under significant strain and his approval rating at a record low of 33 percent. Critics across the political spectrum have raised alarm over the wedding strike and the broader trajectory of the conflict, while administration supporters argue the "tanker for tanker" policy is necessary to deter Iranian aggression and protect global oil flows through the strait.

stories.headline: Gloria Steinem, Feminist Icon and Co-Founder of Ms. Magazine, Dies at 92
stories.summary:
Gloria Steinem, one of the most prominent figures of the American women's liberation movement, died peacefully at her home in New York City, her foundation announced Wednesday. She was 92 and was surrounded by loved ones at the time of her death.

Steinem co-founded Ms. magazine in 1972, one of the first major publications to cover women's issues beyond housekeeping and beauty, and co-founded the Women's Action Alliance to combat sexism. Over five decades she was a leading voice for reproductive rights, equal pay, same-sex marriage legalization, and opposition to the death penalty and female genital mutilation. She witnessed both the 1973 Roe v. Wade ruling and its 2022 reversal.

Born in Toledo, Ohio in 1934, Steinem began her journalism career in New York in the early 1960s, breaking through with an exposé on Playboy Bunny working conditions before becoming a columnist for New York Magazine. Her foundation said she "continued working for equality until the very end," welcoming guests to her home for "Talking Circles" and completing a forthcoming book, An Unexpected Life.

"Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard," her foundation said in a statement. "Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves."

stories.headline: Trump Becomes First Living President on U.S. Currency in a Century With New $1 Coin
stories.summary:
The U.S. Mint on Wednesday launched a $1 coin bearing a portrait of President Donald Trump, making him the first living president to appear on American currency in roughly 100 years. The coins, which have a golden color but contain no actual gold, were released to commemorate America's 250th anniversary and sold out within hours on the Mint's website.

Federal law generally prohibits a living president from appearing on U.S. currency, but the administration used a design clause in the anniversary legislation to overcome the prohibition. The coins appear to be covered by the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020, which bans portraits of living people on the reverse side of coins but does not explicitly address the obverse, where Trump's likeness appears. The coins are priced at $61 for a roll of 25 and are legal tender, though the Mint said they are not being put into general circulation.

The last living president to appear on U.S. currency was Calvin Coolidge, whose portrait appeared on a commemorative half-dollar issued for America's 150th anniversary in 1926. The Trump administration has pursued several similar moves: in March, the Treasury announced paper money would soon bear Trump's signature, and in May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the department was planning a new $250 bill with Trump's portrait.

Critics have characterized the moves as an unprecedented personalization of national institutions for political purposes, while supporters describe them as fitting commemorations of the nation's semiquincentennial milestone.

stories.headline: Update: Chevron Confirms Venezuela Operations Expansion Following Trump Oil Deal
stories.summary:
Oil giant Chevron confirmed Wednesday it will expand its operations in Venezuela following President Trump's announcement of an ambitious concession deal to develop the country's vast oil reserves, with the Pentagon taking a stake in the profits. The confirmation gives new commercial substance to the 100-year oil concession deal covering an estimated 65 billion barrels that was announced earlier this week.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright traveled to Venezuela to promote the deal publicly, and NBC News reported from the scene. The agreement has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and foreign policy analysts who question the wisdom of deepening economic ties with Caracas and the precedent of giving the Defense Department a direct financial interest in foreign oil production.

The deal comes as former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife separately asked a U.S. federal judge Wednesday to dismiss drug trafficking indictments against them, arguing they have immunity as leaders of a foreign country — a legal maneuver that underscores the complicated diplomatic backdrop surrounding U.S.-Venezuela relations.
